nameStory: This striking plant gets its "globe-thistle" name from its perfectly round, spiky flower heads that look like medieval maces or porcupine balls. The "glandular" part refers to the tiny, sticky glands on its stems and leaves that you can actually feel when you touch them. Despite the name, it's not a true thistle at all, but belongs to the same family as sunflowers and daisies!
description: Glandular Globe-thistle is a tall, dramatic perennial that can reach 3-6 feet high with an architectural presence in the garden. Its most striking feature is its collection of steel-blue to pale blue spherical flower heads, each about the size of a golf ball, sitting atop sturdy branching stems. The deeply lobed leaves are grayish-green and covered in white woolly hairs underneath, giving the whole plant a silvery appearance. This European native has escaped cultivation and occasionally pops up in wild spaces across New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Perfectly spherical flower heads about 1-2 inches across, densely packed with small tubular flowers in steel-blue to pale whitish-blue. Each globe feels prickly to the touch, like a spiky ball, and sits alone at the end of a branch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided leaves with spiny-toothed lobes, dark green above but covered in dense white woolly hairs underneath that feel soft and cottony. The upper leaves are smaller and less divided than the large basal leaves.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright plant reaching 3-6 feet with stout, branching stems that feel sticky due to tiny glands. The plant has a bold, architectural appearance with flower globes held high above the foliage.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, ribbed stems that feel noticeably sticky or glandular when touched, often with a grayish appearance. The stickiness comes from tiny resinous glands that may leave a slight residue on your fingers.

habitat: In New England, Glandular Globe-thistle is occasionally found as an garden escape in disturbed soils, roadsides, and field edges, particularly in well-drained, sunny locations. It prefers somewhat poor, alkaline soils and full sun exposure. With only 7 recorded observations in New England, it's quite rare in our region and most likely to be spotted near old homesteads or abandoned gardens where it may persist from cultivation.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as rosettes of deeply divided, woolly leaves. The plant begins its dramatic upward growth, with stems becoming noticeably sticky as they elongate.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time when the spectacular blue globe flowers are most prominent, typically from July through August. The spherical flower heads are at their most vibrant blue and attract numerous bees and butterflies.
seasonality.fall: Flower heads fade to brown but retain their perfect spherical shape, becoming dried ornamental features. The woolly leaves may begin to yellow, but the architectural stem structure remains prominent.
seasonality.winter: The dried stems and globe-shaped seed heads persist, creating striking winter silhouettes. These papery brown spheres often remain intact through snow and can help with identification even in the dormant season.

funFact: Each "globe" is actually made up of hundreds of tiny individual flowers, and when the plant goes to seed, these spheres literally explode apart like botanical fireworks, shooting their seeds in all directions with enough force that you can actually hear the "pop" on a quiet day!
confusionNotes: The perfectly round, spiky flower heads make this nearly impossible to confuse with anything else in New England. True thistles have different flower shapes and much spinier leaves, while other blue wildflowers lack the distinctive globe shape.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "thistle," this plant isn't related to true thistles at all - it's actually in the sunflower family. The confusion comes from both having spiky features, but Globe-thistles are much more ornamental and less aggressive than their prickly namesakes.
compareHints: Glandular Globe-thistle differs from its globe-thistle relatives by having noticeably sticky, glandular stems that you can feel when touched, and paler blue to whitish flower heads. Blue Globe-thistle has deeper blue flowers and non-glandular stems, while Tall Globe-thistle is larger overall but lacks the prominent glandular stickiness that makes this species distinctive.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Blue Globe-thistle can be distinguished from its globe-thistle relatives by its intense steel-blue color and moderate height.
Tall Globe-thistle lives up to its name by being significantly taller than its globe-thistle relatives - often reaching 6 feet compared to the 2-3 feet of Blue Globe-thistle.
